questions.q: Aldehydes are generally more reactive than ketones towards nucleophilic addition because:
options: aldehydes have a higher molar mass
ketones have two alkyl groups that reduce the positive charge on the carbonyl carbon and crowd it
questions.solution:
Two reasons, both favouring aldehydes.

**Electronic**: alkyl groups push electrons onto the carbonyl carbon, so a ketone's carbon, with two of them, is less positive.

**Steric**: two alkyl groups crowd the approach of the nucleophile more than one alkyl group and a small hydrogen.

Tollens' reagent, ammoniacal silver nitrate, is reduced by **aldehydes** to a silver mirror. Ketones do not reduce it.

So ethanal gives the mirror and propanone does not.

Aldol condensation needs an **α-hydrogen**, which the base removes to make a carbanion.

Ethanal, $\mathrm{CH_3CHO}$, has three. Methanal, benzaldehyde and 2,2-dimethylpropanal have none; they undergo the Cannizzaro reaction instead.

questions.q: In the Cannizzaro reaction of benzaldehyde with conc. NaOH, the products are:
questions.solution:
An aldehyde with no α-hydrogen **disproportionates**: one molecule is oxidised, another reduced.

$2\mathrm{C_6H_5CHO} + \mathrm{NaOH} \rightarrow \mathrm{C_6H_5CH_2OH} + \mathrm{C_6H_5COONa}$.

questions.q: Clemmensen reduction converts a carbonyl group to a $\mathrm{CH_2}$ group using:
questions.solution:
**Clemmensen**: Zn–Hg with conc. HCl, suited to compounds stable in acid.

**Wolff–Kishner**: hydrazine with KOH in ethylene glycol, suited to compounds stable in base. Both give the hydrocarbon; $\mathrm{LiAlH_4}$ stops at the alcohol.

Chlorine atoms pull electron density away through the chain (**–I effect**), spreading the negative charge on the carboxylate ion and stabilising it.

More chlorines means a stronger effect, so **trichloroacetic acid** is strongest, with $\mathrm{p}K_a$ about 0.7, against 4.76 for acetic acid.

questions.q: Which compound gives a positive iodoform test?
questions.solution:
The test needs a $\mathrm{CH_3CO}{-}$ group (or $\mathrm{CH_3CH(OH)}{-}$, which is oxidised to one).

**Propanone**, $\mathrm{CH_3COCH_3}$, has it and gives yellow $\mathrm{CHI_3}$. Propanal and pentan-3-one have ethyl groups beside the carbonyl, not methyl.

options: an acid chloride to an aldehyde
questions.solution:
$\mathrm{RCOCl} + \mathrm{H_2} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{Pd/BaSO_4}} \mathrm{RCHO} + \mathrm{HCl}$.

The $\mathrm{BaSO_4}$ **poisons** the palladium so the reduction stops at the **aldehyde** instead of going on to the alcohol.

questions.q: Carboxylic acids do not give the typical reactions of the carbonyl group because:
options: resonance with the –OH group reduces the electrophilic character of the carbonyl carbon
questions.solution:
The lone pair on the –OH oxygen is **delocalised onto the carbonyl**, so the carbonyl carbon is much less positive.

So carboxylic acids do not form oximes, hydrazones or cyanohydrins the way aldehydes and ketones do.

questions.q: How many carbon atoms are there in one molecule of 3-methylbutanal?
questions.solution: Butanal contributes a four-carbon chain; the methyl group adds one more: **5** carbons, $\mathrm{(CH_3)_2CHCH_2CHO}$.

questions.q: Two molecules of ethanal undergo aldol addition. How many carbon atoms does the product 3-hydroxybutanal contain?
questions.solution:
The carbanion from one ethanal adds to the carbonyl of the other, joining two 2-carbon units: **4** carbons, $\mathrm{CH_3CH(OH)CH_2CHO}$.

On heating it loses water to give but-2-enal, crotonaldehyde.

questions.q: What mass of silver, in grams, is deposited when $0.1\,\mathrm{mol}$ of ethanal is completely oxidised by Tollens' reagent? (Ag $= 108$.)
questions.solution:
$\mathrm{RCHO} + 2[\mathrm{Ag(NH_3)_2}]^+ + 3\mathrm{OH^-} \rightarrow \mathrm{RCOO^-} + 2\mathrm{Ag} + 4\mathrm{NH_3} + 2\mathrm{H_2O}$.

Each mole of aldehyde deposits 2 mol of Ag, so $0.2$ mol, which is $0.2 \times 108 = \mathbf{21.6\,g}$.

questions.q: What volume of $\mathrm{CO_2}$, in litres at STP, is evolved when $0.5\,\mathrm{mol}$ of acetic acid reacts completely with excess sodium bicarbonate? (1 mol of gas at STP $= 22.4\,\mathrm{L}$.)
questions.solution:
$\mathrm{CH_3COOH} + \mathrm{NaHCO_3} \rightarrow \mathrm{CH_3COONa} + \mathrm{H_2O} + \mathrm{CO_2}$: one mole of acid, one mole of gas.

$0.5 \times 22.4 = \mathbf{11.2\,L}$. This brisk effervescence is the test for a carboxylic acid; phenols are too weak to give it.

questions.q: The $\mathrm{p}K_a$ of acetic acid is $4.76$ and that of formic acid is $3.75$. By roughly what whole-number factor is formic acid the stronger acid? (Use $10^{1.01} \approx 10$.)
questions.solution:
$\dfrac{K_a(\mathrm{HCOOH})}{K_a(\mathrm{CH_3COOH})} = 10^{4.76 - 3.75} = 10^{1.01} \approx \mathbf{10}$.

The methyl group in acetic acid pushes electrons onto the carboxylate and destabilises it; formic acid has a hydrogen there.

questions.q: Explain the following with one equation each: (a) aldol condensation, (b) Cannizzaro reaction, (c) Hell–Volhard–Zelinsky reaction, (d) decarboxylation, (e) Wolff–Kishner reduction.
questions.solution:
**(a) Aldol condensation.** An aldehyde or ketone with an α-hydrogen, in dilute alkali, forms a β-hydroxy carbonyl compound, which loses water on heating.

$2\mathrm{CH_3CHO} \xrightarrow{\text{dil. NaOH}} \mathrm{CH_3CH(OH)CH_2CHO} \xrightarrow{\Delta} \mathrm{CH_3CH{=}CHCHO}$

**(b) Cannizzaro reaction.** An aldehyde with no α-hydrogen, in conc. alkali, is half oxidised and half reduced.

$2\mathrm{HCHO} + \mathrm{NaOH} \rightarrow \mathrm{CH_3OH} + \mathrm{HCOONa}$

**(c) Hell–Volhard–Zelinsky reaction.** A carboxylic acid with an α-hydrogen is halogenated at the α-carbon by $\mathrm{Cl_2}$ or $\mathrm{Br_2}$ with red phosphorus.

$\mathrm{CH_3COOH} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{Cl_2}/\text{red P}} \mathrm{ClCH_2COOH}$

**(d) Decarboxylation.** The sodium salt of an acid heated with soda lime (NaOH + CaO) loses $\mathrm{CO_2}$ and gives an alkane with one carbon fewer.

$\mathrm{CH_3COONa} + \mathrm{NaOH} \xrightarrow{\text{CaO}, \Delta} \mathrm{CH_4} + \mathrm{Na_2CO_3}$

**(e) Wolff–Kishner reduction.** The carbonyl compound forms a hydrazone, which, heated with KOH in ethylene glycol, loses $\mathrm{N_2}$ to give the hydrocarbon.

$\mathrm{CH_3COCH_3} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{NH_2NH_2}} \mathrm{(CH_3)_2C{=}NNH_2} \xrightarrow{\text{KOH}, \Delta} \mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_3} + \mathrm{N_2}$
